title: Columbus Lands in the Bahamas
description: Christopher Columbus makes landfall in the Caribbean, initiating transatlantic contact between Europe and the Americas.
cause: Spanish desire for maritime wealth and competition with Portugal for trade routes drove Columbus's westward voyage.
effect: Initiated the Columbian Exchange and began the catastrophic demise of indigenous populations via disease.
causes: Spanish desire for maritime wealth
Trade route competition with Portugal
Ottoman control of overland Asian routes
effects: Demise of indigenous populations via disease
Initiation of the Columbian Exchange
Spanish global hegemony
significance: Permanently connected the Eastern and Western Hemispheres
Shifted global economic power to Western Europe

title: Treaty of Tordesillas
description: Spain and Portugal agreed by treaty to divide newly discovered lands along a line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands, moving westward the line Pope Alexander VI had drawn in 1493.
cause: Catholic desire to prevent war between two major Iberian naval empires competing for new territories.
effect: Spain dominated the Americas while Portugal secured Brazil and African trade routes.
causes: Catholic desire to prevent war between two major Iberian naval empires
effects: Spain dominates the Americas
Portugal secures Brazil and African trade routes
significance: Established early geopolitical boundaries that shaped colonial language and cultural landscapes

title: Encomienda System Established
description: Royal grants gave Spanish conquistadors the right to indigenous labor in exchange for Christianization.
cause: The Spanish crown needed to extract mineral wealth and agricultural products without paying labor wages.
effect: Brutal enslavement and massive population decline of Native Americans followed.
causes: Spanish crown's need to extract mineral wealth and agricultural products without paying labor wages
effects: Brutal enslavement and massive population decline of Native Americans
significance: Established a rigid, race-based social hierarchy
Set a precedent for coercive labor systems in the Americas

title: Valladolid Debate
description: A theological debate between Bartolomé de Las Casas and Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda addressed the rights and humanity of indigenous peoples.
cause: Growing criticism of Spanish cruelty toward Native Americans by religious figures like Las Casas.
effect: Minimal immediate legal changes resulted, but it contributed to the 'Black Legend' of Spanish cruelty.
causes: Growing criticism of Spanish cruelty toward Native Americans by religious figures like Las Casas
effects: Minimal immediate legal changes
Contributed to the 'Black Legend' of Spanish cruelty
significance: The first moral debate in European history regarding the treatment and humanity of colonized peoples

title: Roanoke Colony Founded
description: Sir Walter Raleigh attempted to establish the first permanent English settlement in the Americas.
cause: English ambition to counter Spanish wealth and establish a naval base in the New World.
effect: The 1585 colonists abandoned Roanoke and sailed home with Francis Drake in 1586; a second colony planted in 1587 vanished, becoming 'The Lost Colony'.
causes: English ambition to counter Spanish wealth and establish a naval base in the New World
effects: First colony abandoned in 1586, the later 1587 colony lost
Financial loss for investors
Pushed England toward joint-stock funding for later colonies
significance: Illustrated the vulnerability of early, underfunded colonization attempts
Forced England to rethink settlement strategies

title: Acoma Pueblo Massacre
description: Juan de Oñate brutally crushed Pueblo resistance at Acoma in modern-day New Mexico.
cause: The Pueblo at Acoma refused to hand over seasonal food supplies to Spanish conquistadors.
effect: Mass casualties, enslavement, and the symbolic severing of feet for surviving Pueblo men followed.
causes: Pueblo refusal to hand over seasonal food supplies to Spanish conquistadors
effects: Casualties, enslavement, and the symbolic severing of feet for surviving Pueblo men
significance: Demonstrated the extreme violence used by the Spanish to enforce the encomienda and assert colonial control

title: Founding of Jamestown
description: The Virginia Company established the first permanent English settlement in North America.
cause: English investors sought gold, silver, and a northwest passage via joint-stock financing.
effect: Survived the 'Starving Time' and found economic salvation in tobacco cultivation.
causes: English investors seeking gold, silver, and a northwest passage via joint-stock financing
effects: 'Starving Time' nearly destroyed the colony
Conflict with the Powhatan Confederacy
Eventual discovery of tobacco as a cash crop
significance: Launched the English colonial empire in North America
Established a blueprint for corporate settlement

title: House of Burgesses & First Enslaved Africans Arrive
description: Virginia established a representative assembly while a Dutch ship traded 20 captive Africans for supplies.
cause: The need for local governance to attract settlers and a severe labor shortage in booming tobacco fields.
effect: Simultaneously established precedents for self-rule and for race-based chattel slavery.
causes: Need for local governance to attract settlers
Severe labor shortage in booming tobacco fields
effects: Precedent for self-rule
Initial steps toward legal, lifelong, race-based chattel slavery
significance: Simultaneously planted the roots of American representative democracy and institutional systemic racism

title: Mayflower Compact
description: Pilgrims aboard the Mayflower signed a self-governing agreement establishing a democratic colony in Plymouth.
cause: The Pilgrims had no legal authority to settle in the area and needed a governing framework to maintain order.
effect: Established an early precedent for self-governance and majority rule in the American colonies.
causes: Pilgrims lacked a royal charter for their landing site
Fear of mutiny without a governing structure
effects: Created a precedent for written self-government in North America
Majority-rule principle influenced later colonial governance
significance: One of the first examples of self-governance in North America
Foreshadowed the democratic principles embedded in the Constitution

title: Massachusetts Bay Colony Founded
description: Puritans led by John Winthrop launched a large-scale religious settlement in New England.
cause: Religious persecution in England under King Charles I and the desire to build a model Christian society.
effect: Triggered the Great Migration of families and established a highly ordered, church-centric society.
causes: Religious persecution in England under King Charles I
Desire to build a model Christian society
effects: Great Migration of families
Establishment of a highly ordered, church-centric society
significance: Promoted the cultural concept of American 'exceptionalism' via Winthrop's 'City Upon a Hill' sermon

title: Roger Williams Banned / Rhode Island Founded
description: Dissident minister Roger Williams was banished from Massachusetts for advocating separation of church and state.
cause: Puritan intolerance of religious dissent and Williams's defense of Native American land rights.
effect: Williams founded Providence and established complete religious freedom and separation of church and state.
causes: Puritan intolerance of religious dissent
Williams's defense of Native American land rights
effects: Founding of Providence
Establishment of complete religious freedom and separation of church and state
significance: Created a safe haven for free thought
Set a structural precedent for the First Amendment

title: Maryland Toleration Act
description: Colonial law guaranteed religious freedom to all Trinitarian Christians in Maryland.
cause: Lord Baltimore's desire to protect minority Catholics from a growing Protestant majority.
effect: Provided temporary political stability before being repealed during a Protestant-led rebellion.
causes: Lord Baltimore's desire to protect minority Catholics from a growing Protestant majority
effects: Temporary political stability
Later repealed during a Protestant-led local rebellion
significance: An early, foundational stepping stone toward institutionalized religious freedom in North America

title: Navigation Acts
description: England enacted mercantilist laws requiring colonial trade to flow through English ships and ports.
cause: England sought to consolidate economic control over its colonies and exclude Dutch traders.
effect: Fueled resentment in the colonies and contributed to a tradition of smuggling and resistance to British authority.
causes: England wanted to profit from colonial trade under mercantilism
Competition with Dutch shipping threatened English commercial dominance
effects: Colonial smuggling became widespread
Planted seeds of resentment toward British economic control
significance: Embodied mercantilist imperial policy toward the colonies
Created long-term colonial grievances that contributed to the Revolution

title: English Capture of New Amsterdam (New York)
description: English naval forces seized the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam without firing a shot.
cause: English commercial jealousy and the desire to close the geographic gap between New England and the Chesapeake.
effect: Dutch settlers were assimilated while diverse trading hubs and English commerce expanded.
causes: English commercial jealousy
Desire to close the geographic gap between New England and the Chesapeake
effects: Assimilation of Dutch settlers
Preservation of diverse trading hubs
Expansion of English commerce
significance: Consolidated English geopolitical control over the Atlantic seaboard from Maine to the Carolinas

title: King Philip's War (Metacom's War)
description: A multi-tribal alliance attacked New England towns in the bloodiest per-capita colonial conflict.
cause: Continuous English encroachment on Native American lands and the hanging of three Wampanoag men.
effect: Mass casualties on both sides and the destruction of southern New England tribal autonomy.
causes: Continuous English encroachment on Native American lands
Hanging of three Wampanoag men
effects: High casualties on both sides
Metacom's death
Destruction of southern New England tribal autonomy
significance: The costliest war in per-capita colonial history
Ended organized indigenous resistance in New England

title: Bacon's Rebellion
description: Nathaniel Bacon led armed Virginia colonists against Governor Berkeley and Native Americans on the frontier.
cause: Frontier settlers were angered by Berkeley's refusal to protect them from Native American raids and by elite political control.
effect: Led planters to shift from indentured servants to enslaved Africans as a more controllable labor force.
causes: Elite political corruption under Governor Berkeley
Frustrated indentured servants with no land access after completing service
effects: Planters shifted to enslaved African labor to avoid future rebellions by freed servants
Revealed deep class tensions in colonial Virginia
significance: Pivotal turning point accelerating the growth of race-based slavery in Virginia
Demonstrated the dangers of a large class of discontented, landless colonists

title: Pueblo Revolt (Popé's Rebellion)
description: Popé and allied Pueblo communities launched a coordinated uprising across New Mexico in August 1680, killing roughly 400 colonists and driving Spanish survivors south to El Paso.
cause: Franciscan campaigns to stamp out Pueblo ceremonies, combined with forced labor demands and years of drought and raiding, pushed normally separate villages into a single alliance.
effect: Spanish authority in New Mexico collapsed for twelve years until Diego de Vargas retook the province in 1692.
causes: Franciscan suppression of Pueblo religious ceremonies
Forced labor and tribute under Spanish colonial rule
Drought, famine, and raids the Spanish failed to prevent
effects: Roughly 400 colonists killed and 2,000 survivors expelled
Spanish driven out of New Mexico for twelve years
Open restoration of Pueblo religious practice
significance: The most successful Native uprising against a European power in North America
Forced Spain to moderate religious and labor demands after the 1692 reconquest

title: Pennsylvania Founded
description: William Penn established a proprietary colony as a refuge for Quakers based on religious tolerance.
cause: A royal debt owed to Penn's family and the Quaker desire to escape intense persecution in England.
effect: Rapid population growth due to religious tolerance and peaceful early relations with local tribes.
causes: Royal debt owed to Penn's family
Quaker desire to escape intense persecution in England
effects: Rapid population growth due to religious tolerance
Peaceful early relations with local tribes
Grid-based urban planning
significance: Demonstrated that a diverse, tolerant, and pacifist colony could achieve immense economic success

title: Glorious Revolution / English Bill of Rights
description: England's Protestant monarchs William and Mary accepted parliamentary supremacy, reshaping colonial charters.
cause: Protestant opposition to the Catholic King James II forced his abdication.
effect: Strengthened colonial assemblies and reinforced the concept of constitutional limits on government power.
causes: Protestant fears of Catholic rule under James II
Parliament sought supremacy over the monarchy
effects: Colonial assemblies gained more independence from royal governors
Established constitutional monarchy as England's governing model
significance: Reinforced the idea that government authority derives from law, not divine right
Influenced the political philosophy behind the American Revolution

title: Salem Witch Trials
description: A wave of witchcraft accusations in Salem, Massachusetts led to twenty executions.
cause: Social tensions, religious anxiety, and political instability in Puritan Massachusetts created a climate of fear.
effect: Weakened the authority of Puritan clergy and prompted greater skepticism of spectral evidence in courts.
causes: Social and economic tensions between Salem Village and Salem Town
Political instability after the revocation of the Massachusetts Bay Charter
effects: Discredited use of spectral evidence in legal proceedings
Accelerated decline of Puritan theocratic authority in New England
significance: Illustrated the dangers of religious extremism and mob mentality
Marked a turning point toward greater legal rationalism in the colonies

title: Stono Rebellion
description: About twenty enslaved people, led by a man called Jemmy, seized weapons near the Stono River in South Carolina and marched south toward Spanish Florida, gathering some sixty followers.
cause: Spanish Florida's standing offer of freedom to those who fled British colonies gave South Carolina's enslaved majority a concrete destination.
effect: Colonial militia overtook and killed most of the rebels within days, and the colony answered with the punishing Negro Act of 1740.
causes: Spanish Florida's promise of freedom to fugitives from British colonies
Enslaved people outnumbering whites across the lowcountry
Brutal labor conditions on rice plantations
effects: Roughly twenty colonists and dozens of rebels killed
Passage of the 1740 Negro Act restricting movement and assembly
Prohibitive duties imposed to slow African imports
significance: The largest slave uprising in the mainland British colonies
Hardened South Carolina's slave code and outlawed teaching enslaved people to write

title: First Great Awakening
description: A wave of emotional Protestant revivals swept the colonies through the 1730s and 1740s, cresting around 1740 as George Whitefield drew enormous crowds on his preaching tours.
cause: Revivalists such as Jonathan Edwards and Whitefield reacted against what they saw as cooling piety and empty formalism in established colonial churches.
effect: Congregations fractured into revivalist 'New Lights' and traditionalist 'Old Lights' across multiple denominations.
causes: Perceived decline of religious fervor in established churches
Enlightenment rationalism challenging traditional doctrine
Itinerant preachers and cheap print carrying revival news between colonies
effects: New Light and Old Light splits within colonial denominations
Founding of new colleges including Princeton and Dartmouth
Surging Baptist and Presbyterian membership
significance: The first mass movement experienced across colonial boundaries
Encouraged ordinary colonists to question inherited religious and political authority

title: Albany Congress
description: Seven colonies met to coordinate defense against France and secure Iroquois loyalty ahead of the French and Indian War.
cause: Looming threat of French military expansion in the Ohio River Valley.
effect: Colonies rejected Franklin's Albany Plan of Union, unwilling to surrender control of taxation.
causes: Looming threat of French military expansion in the Ohio River Valley
British demand for a united colonial response
Franklin's May 1754 'Join, or Die' cartoon had already primed colonists for union
effects: Rejection of the Albany Plan of Union by colonies fearing loss of taxation power
Failure to secure a lasting alliance with the Iroquois Confederacy
significance: The most ambitious early attempt at intercolonial unity
First plan to unite nearly all the mainland colonies under a central government

title: French and Indian War
description: Britain and its colonial allies defeated France and its Native allies in a conflict over North American territory.
cause: Competing British and French territorial claims in the Ohio River Valley escalated into open warfare.
effect: Britain gained vast territory but accumulated massive debt, leading to new colonial taxes that sparked revolution.
causes: French expansion into the Ohio River Valley threatened British colonists
Both empires sought dominance over the lucrative fur trade
effects: Britain doubled its territorial holdings in North America
War debt prompted Britain to tax the colonies, igniting the Revolution
significance: Transformed North American politics by eliminating French power east of the Mississippi
Directly triggered the taxation disputes that led to American independence

title: Pontiac's Rebellion & Proclamation of 1763
description: A Native American alliance attacked British forts while King George III banned colonial settlement west of the Appalachians.
cause: Indian anger over harsh British postwar policies and the British desire to prevent costly frontier Indian wars.
effect: Colonial outrage and widespread defiance of the border line deepened distrust of British imperial authority.
causes: Indian anger over harsh British postwar policies
British desire to prevent costly frontier Indian wars
effects: Colonial outrage
Widespread defiance of the border line
Deep distrust of British imperial authority
significance: Marked the end of salutary neglect
Initiated a cycle of mutual distrust leading to independence

title: Stamp Act
description: Britain imposed a direct tax on printed materials in the colonies to help pay war debts.
cause: Britain needed revenue after the French and Indian War and believed colonists should help pay for their defense.
effect: United colonial opposition under the 'no taxation without representation' slogan and led to the Stamp Act Congress.
causes: Britain's £140 million war debt after the French and Indian War
British belief that colonists should contribute to their own defense costs
effects: Sparked colonial boycotts of British goods
Led to the Stamp Act Congress, the first intercolonial body the colonies convened on their own initiative
significance: First direct internal tax on colonists, violating their tradition of self-taxation
Crystallized the 'no taxation without representation' principle

title: Boston Massacre
description: British soldiers fired into a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people.
cause: Tensions between Boston residents and British troops stationed in the city had been escalating for months.
effect: Inflamed anti-British sentiment; Paul Revere's engraving became a powerful piece of revolutionary propaganda.
causes: Resentment over the Quartering Act forcing colonists to house British troops
Economic tensions caused by the presence of soldiers competing for jobs
effects: Paul Revere's propaganda engraving shaped colonial public opinion against Britain
Accelerated the push toward colonial independence
significance: Turned a street brawl into a rallying symbol for colonial resistance
Demonstrated the power of print media in shaping political opinion

title: Boston Tea Party
description: Colonial protesters dumped 342 chests of British East India Company tea into Boston Harbor.
cause: The Tea Act gave the East India Company a monopoly and colonists protested taxation without representation.
effect: Prompted Britain to pass the Intolerable Acts, which further unified colonial resistance.
causes: The Tea Act threatened colonial merchants by granting a monopoly to the East India Company
Colonists rejected Parliament's right to tax them without representation
effects: Britain responded with the Coercive (Intolerable) Acts, closing Boston Harbor
Twelve colonies sent representatives to the First Continental Congress
significance: Transformed protest from economic boycott to direct political defiance
Brought colonies closer to unified resistance against British authority

title: First Continental Congress
description: Twelve colonies met in Philadelphia to organize a unified response to British punishments.
cause: Parliament's passage of the Intolerable Acts to crush Massachusetts after the Boston Tea Party.
effect: Created The Association to enforce total boycotts and formally declared colonial rights.
causes: Parliament's passage of the Intolerable Acts to crush Massachusetts
effects: Creation of The Association to enforce total boycotts
Declaration of colonial rights
Agreement to meet again
significance: Advanced intercolonial unity from loose protest groups into a functional, de facto national governing body

title: Battles of Lexington and Concord
description: The first military engagements of the Revolutionary War between British troops and colonial militias.
cause: British troops were ordered to seize the colonial military stores at Concord; colonists also believed the column meant to arrest Samuel Adams and John Hancock.
effect: The 'Shot heard round the world' triggered the mobilization of colonial militias across the region.
causes: British troops ordered to seize colonial weapons stockpiles and arrest rebel leaders in Concord
effects: 'Shot heard round the world'
British retreat under heavy guerrilla fire
Mobilization of colonial militias
significance: Crossed the point of no return from political protest to open, bloody revolutionary war

title: Declaration of Independence
description: The Second Continental Congress formally declared the thirteen colonies independent from Britain.
cause: Escalating military conflict, failed petitions to the Crown, and Enlightenment ideas inspired the break.
effect: Established Enlightenment principles—equality, natural rights, consent of the governed—as the foundation of American political thought.
causes: Continued military conflict after Lexington and Concord
Thomas Paine's Common Sense shifted public opinion toward independence
effects: Established Enlightenment ideals of natural rights as the basis of American government
Provided a framework for evaluating American democracy across history
significance: Articulated a universal theory of human rights that influenced revolutions worldwide
Remains the founding statement of American political identity

title: Battle of Saratoga
description: Continental forces surrounded and captured a major British army in upstate New York.
cause: A failed British multi-pronged strategy to isolate New England from the rest of the colonies.
effect: Boosted American morale and convinced France to sign a formal military alliance against Britain.
causes: Failed British multi-pronged strategy to isolate New England from the rest of the colonies
effects: Boosted American morale
Convinced France to sign a formal military alliance against Britain
significance: The definitive military turning point of the war
Transformed a colonial rebellion into a global conflict

title: Articles of Confederation Ratified
description: The first U.S. constitution created a weak central government with most power reserved to the states.
cause: States feared a powerful central government after their experience under British rule.
effect: Proved inadequate for governing the new nation, leading to the Constitutional Convention of 1787.
causes: States feared that a strong central government would replicate British tyranny
Revolutionary ideology emphasized local self-governance
effects: Congress could not tax, regulate commerce, or enforce laws effectively
Shays' Rebellion exposed the weakness of the national government
significance: First attempt at national self-governance in America
Its failures directly led to the creation of the stronger Constitution of 1787

title: Treaty of Paris (1783)
description: The peace treaty ending the Revolutionary War granted formal British recognition of U.S. independence.
cause: British defeat at Yorktown and rising financial strains and political opposition within Great Britain.
effect: Formal British recognition of U.S. independence and the American western border set at the Mississippi River.
causes: British defeat at Yorktown
Rising financial strains and political opposition within Great Britain
effects: Formal British recognition of U.S. independence
American western border set at the Mississippi River
significance: Secured American sovereignty
Doubled the territorial size of the infant republic overnight

title: Shays' Rebellion
description: An armed uprising of indebted western Massachusetts farmers exposed the fatal weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation.
cause: High state taxes, aggressive home foreclosures, and the imprisonment of debtors by eastern elites.
effect: Exposed the inability of the weak national government under the Articles to raise a military force quickly.
causes: High state taxes
Aggressive home foreclosures
Imprisonment of debtors by eastern elites
effects: Shutdown of local courts
Inability of the weak national government under the Articles to raise a military force quickly
significance: Convinced national elites that the Articles of Confederation were too weak
Catalyzed the call for a new Constitution

title: Constitutional Convention & Northwest Ordinance
description: Delegates wrote a new governing charter while Congress created a system for admitting new western states and banned slavery north of the Ohio River.
cause: Total failure of the Articles of Confederation and disputes over western land claims and congressional representation.
effect: Produced the Great Compromise, the Three-Fifths Compromise, and a clear pathway for westward statehood.
causes: Total failure of the Articles of Confederation
Disputes over western land claims and congressional representation
effects: Great Compromise (bicameralism)
Three-Fifths Compromise
Establishment of a clear path for statehood
significance: Replaced a weak league of friendship with a strong, flexible, federal constitutional government

title: U.S. Constitution Ratified
description: Nine states ratified the new Constitution, replacing the Articles of Confederation.
cause: Shays' Rebellion and economic instability under the Articles revealed the need for stronger central authority.
effect: Created the federal system with separation of powers that remains the framework of American government.
causes: Economic chaos and Shays' Rebellion demonstrated the Articles' failures
Commercial interests demanded a stable national currency and trade rules
effects: Created a federal government with the power to tax, regulate commerce, and enforce laws
Established the separation of powers and checks and balances
significance: Created the world's oldest surviving written national constitution
Defined the balance between federal authority and states' rights that still shapes American politics

title: Hamilton's Financial Plan
description: Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton proposed paying federal debt at full value and having the national government assume the states' Revolutionary War debts to establish public credit.
cause: The new government inherited roughly $77 million in unpaid war debt and had no established credit with foreign lenders.
effect: Southern opposition eased only after the Compromise of 1790 traded assumption for placing the permanent capital on the Potomac.
causes: Roughly $77 million in unpaid Revolutionary War debt
Federal credit too poor to borrow abroad on favorable terms
Hamilton's belief that wealthy creditors would invest in a solvent government
effects: Funding Act and debt assumption passed in 1790
Residence Act sited the capital on the Potomac
Excise taxes, including the 1791 whiskey tax, funded repayment
significance: Established American public credit and a precedent for broad federal economic power
Opposition from Jefferson and Madison hardened into the first party system

title: Bill of Rights Ratified
description: The first ten amendments to the Constitution guaranteed individual liberties and limited federal power.
cause: Anti-Federalists demanded explicit protections for individual rights as a condition of ratification.
effect: Established foundational civil liberties that shaped American law and culture.
causes: Anti-Federalists feared a powerful central government would trample individual freedoms
Several states made ratification contingent on adding a bill of rights
effects: Guaranteed fundamental freedoms including speech, religion, and due process
Became the constitutional foundation for civil rights claims across American history
significance: Defined the relationship between the individual and the federal government
Provided legal tools for expanding rights across subsequent centuries

title: Invention of the Cotton Gin
description: Eli Whitney built a machine that stripped seeds from short-staple cotton, cleaning roughly fifty times what a worker could process by hand in a day.
cause: Short-staple cotton grew well across the southern interior, but its clinging seeds made hand cleaning far too slow to be profitable.
effect: Cotton became commercially viable throughout the Deep South, and planters expanded acreage and enslaved labor to plant and pick it.
causes: Clinging seeds made short-staple cotton unprofitable to clean by hand
Rising British textile mill demand for raw cotton
Only coastal long-staple cotton was commercially viable
effects: Cotton cultivation spread rapidly across the Deep South
Sharp increase in demand for enslaved field labor
Cotton became the nation's leading export
significance: Revitalized slavery at the moment many Americans expected it to wither
Bound the southern economy to a single cash crop for generations

title: Whiskey Rebellion
description: Western Pennsylvania farmers violently protested an excise tax on whiskey.
cause: Hamilton's economic plan taxed whiskey, a crucial backcountry currency and trade good.
effect: President Washington personally led 13,000 federal troops to crush the protest; rebels dispersed without a battle.
causes: Hamilton's economic plan taxing a crucial backcountry currency and trade good
effects: President Washington personally leads 13,000 federal troops to crush the protest
Rebels disperse without a battle
significance: Proven demonstration that the new federal government possessed the executive power to enforce its laws

title: Alien and Sedition Acts & Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions
description: Federalists passed four laws targeting immigrants and press criticism of the government; Jefferson and Madison replied with resolutions claiming states could judge federal laws unconstitutional.
cause: War fever during the undeclared naval Quasi-War with France let Federalists cast Republican critics and French immigrants as security threats.
effect: Federal prosecutors jailed Republican editors and a sitting congressman while Kentucky and Virginia issued formal protests.
causes: Quasi-War tensions with France after the XYZ Affair
Federalist fear of French and Irish immigrant voters
Partisan hostility toward Republican newspapers
effects: Prosecution and jailing of Republican editors and Congressman Matthew Lyon
Naturalization residency requirement raised from five to fourteen years
Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions drafted secretly by Jefferson and Madison
significance: Framed an enduring conflict between wartime security and free speech
Supplied the compact theory later invoked by nullifiers and secessionists

title: Election of 1800 ("Revolution of 1800")
description: Democratic-Republican Thomas Jefferson defeated Federalist John Adams in the first peaceful transfer of power between opposing parties.
cause: High taxes from the Quasi-War and intense public anger over the Federalist Alien and Sedition Acts.
effect: Resulted in the first peaceful transfer of power between opposing political parties in American history.
causes: High taxes from the Quasi-War
Intense public anger over the Federalist Alien and Sedition Acts
effects: Peaceful transfer of executive power between opposing political factions
Eventual demise of the Federalist Party
significance: Proved that a constitutional republic could survive a bitter, polarized partisan transition of power

title: Louisiana Purchase
description: The United States purchased approximately 828,000 square miles from France, doubling the nation's size.
cause: Napoleon's military setbacks in Haiti and ambitions in Europe made him eager to sell French North American territory.
effect: Fueled westward expansion, intensified debates over slavery's extension, and raised constitutional questions about presidential power.
causes: Napoleon abandoned his American empire after the Haitian Revolution crushed his army
Jefferson sought control of the Mississippi River and New Orleans for western trade
effects: Doubled the size of the United States
Intensified debates over whether slavery would expand into new territories
significance: Greatest territorial acquisition in American history, enabling westward expansion
Raised unresolved questions about slavery in new territories that would haunt the nation for decades

title: Marbury v. Madison
description: Supreme Court Chief Justice John Marshall struck down a section of the Judiciary Act of 1789, establishing judicial review.
cause: Federalist 'midnight judges' appointments were blocked by the incoming Jefferson administration.
effect: Established the Supreme Court as the final arbiter of constitutional meaning via judicial review.
causes: Federalist 'midnight judges' appointments blocked by incoming Jefferson administration
effects: Established the Supreme Court as the final arbiter of constitutional meaning
significance: Created the doctrine of judicial review
Elevated the judiciary to an equal branch of government

title: Embargo Act
description: Jefferson banned all American exports to foreign ports in response to British and French violations of free seas.
cause: Continued British and French violations of free seas, including impressment of American sailors.
effect: Caused economic devastation for New England merchants and a surge in illegal smuggling.
causes: Continued British and French violations of free seas, including impressment of American sailors
effects: Absolute economic devastation for New England merchants
Surge in illegal smuggling
significance: An unintended catalyst that forced New England to pivot capital into domestic manufacturing and factories

title: War of 1812
description: The United States declared war on Britain over impressment of sailors and British support for Native American resistance.
cause: British violations of American neutrality and impressment of American sailors inflamed public opinion.
effect: Fostered American nationalism and effectively ended significant Native American resistance east of the Mississippi.
causes: British impressment of American sailors into the Royal Navy
British support for Native American confederacies led by Tecumseh threatening U.S. expansion
effects: Sparked an era of American nationalism (the 'Era of Good Feelings')
Destroyed the pan-Indian resistance movement east of the Mississippi after Tecumseh's death
significance: Consolidated U.S. sovereignty and ended British interference in American affairs
Marked the end of viable Native American resistance to U.S. expansion in the East

title: Battle of New Orleans
description: Andrew Jackson's forces won a crushing military victory over veteran British forces after the peace treaty had already been signed.
cause: Slow transatlantic communication delayed news of the Treaty of Ghent while Britain attempted to seize the Mississippi River mouth.
effect: Andrew Jackson was instantly transformed into a legendary national hero, launching his path to the presidency.
causes: Slow transatlantic communication
British attempt to seize control of the Mississippi River mouth
effects: Instant transformation of Andrew Jackson into a legendary national hero
Surge in American pride
significance: Fostered a national myth of American military invincibility
Launched Jackson's political path to the presidency

title: McCulloch v. Maryland
description: The Supreme Court unanimously upheld Congress's power to charter the Second Bank of the United States and voided Maryland's tax on its Baltimore branch.
cause: Maryland taxed the unpopular national bank's local branch, and cashier James McCulloch refused to pay.
effect: Chief Justice Marshall held that the Necessary and Proper Clause grants implied powers and that states cannot tax federal institutions.
causes: Widespread state hostility to the Second Bank chartered in 1816
Maryland's tax designed to drive the branch out of the state
McCulloch's refusal to pay the state tax
effects: Doctrine of implied powers established under the Necessary and Proper Clause
States barred from taxing federal instrumentalities
Federal supremacy affirmed over conflicting state law
significance: Gave Congress broad latitude to act beyond its enumerated powers
Anchored the constitutional doctrine behind later expansions of national authority

title: Missouri Compromise
description: Congress admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state, drawing a line at 36°30'.
cause: Missouri's application for statehood as a slave state threatened the balance of free and slave states in the Senate.
effect: Temporarily settled the slavery expansion debate but established a precedent that would be revisited by later crises.
causes: Missouri's 1819 statehood application threatened to tip the Senate balance toward slave states
Northerners feared the political power of expanding slaveholder representation
effects: Preserved sectional balance in the Senate for three decades
Drew the 36°30' line as a geographic boundary for slavery's expansion
significance: Demonstrated that slavery was becoming the central, unresolvable fault line in American politics
Established the pattern of legislative compromise that delayed but could not prevent civil war

title: Monroe Doctrine
description: President Monroe declared the Western Hemisphere closed to further European colonization or intervention.
cause: The fall of the Spanish Empire and fears that European monarchies would crush new Latin American republics.
effect: Had minimal immediate impact due to weak U.S. Navy, but was respected because of British naval backing.
causes: Fall of the Spanish Empire
Fears that European monarchies would crush new Latin American republics
effects: Minimal immediate impact due to weak U.S. Navy
Respected because of British naval backing
significance: Established the core framework for American foreign policy in the Americas for the next two centuries

title: The "Corrupt Bargain" Election
description: John Quincy Adams won the presidency in the House of Representatives over Andrew Jackson in a controversial deal.
cause: A four-way split in electoral votes led Speaker Henry Clay to throw his support to Adams, who then named Clay Secretary of State.
effect: Intense public anger split the Democratic-Republicans into the Democrats and the National Republicans.
causes: Four-way split in electoral votes
Speaker Henry Clay throws his support to Adams and becomes Secretary of State
effects: Intense public anger
Splitting of the Democratic-Republicans into the Democrats and National Republicans (Whigs)
significance: Ended the 'Era of Good Feelings'
Launched the Second Party System fueled by mass democratic participation

title: Erie Canal Opens
description: A state-funded canal connected the Great Lakes to the Atlantic Ocean via the Hudson River, cutting shipping costs by 90%.
cause: New York's ambition to capture western agricultural commerce in the absence of federal infrastructure funding.
effect: Explosive growth of New York City and a boom in midwestern farming towns followed.
causes: New York's ambition to capture western agricultural commerce
Lack of federal infrastructure funding
effects: Shipping costs drop by 90%
Explosive growth of New York City
Boom in midwestern farming towns
significance: Cemented the economic and political alliance between the industrial Northeast and agricultural Midwest

title: Indian Removal Act
description: Congress authorized the forced relocation of Native American tribes from the Southeast to lands west of the Mississippi.
cause: White settlers demanded fertile southeastern land and the federal government prioritized expansion over Native rights.
effect: Led to the Trail of Tears and the displacement and deaths of tens of thousands of Native Americans.
causes: Discovery of gold in Cherokee territory in Georgia intensified settler demand for Native land
Jackson's political philosophy rejected federal protection of Native sovereignty
effects: Forced removal of the Five Civilized Tribes in the Trail of Tears, killing thousands
Cleared millions of acres for cotton cultivation and slavery's expansion
significance: Represents a defining episode of ethnic cleansing in American history
Established federal precedent for violating treaty obligations with Native nations

title: Second Great Awakening
description: Decades of Protestant revivalism, building from the early 1800s and cresting around 1830, spread camp meetings and the conviction that salvation was an individual choice.
cause: Frontier settlement and rapid market growth left many Americans outside established congregations and receptive to emotional itinerant preaching.
effect: Methodist and Baptist membership soared while converts channeled their zeal into moral reform campaigns.
causes: Frontier settlement beyond the reach of established churches
Market Revolution unsettling traditional communities
Preachers like Charles Finney rejecting predestination for personal choice
effects: Explosive growth of Methodist and Baptist denominations
Frontier camp meetings drawing thousands, from Cane Ridge, Kentucky, onward
New religious movements including the Mormons taking shape
significance: Supplied the moral energy behind temperance, abolition, and women's rights
Democratized American religion around personal conversion rather than clerical authority

title: Garrison Launches The Liberator
description: William Lloyd Garrison began publishing an abolitionist weekly in Boston on January 1, 1831, demanding immediate and unconditional emancipation rather than gradual reform.
cause: Garrison broke with gradualists and colonizationists who proposed resettling free black Americans abroad instead of abolishing slavery outright.
effect: The paper gave radical abolitionism a national voice and provoked furious retaliation from southern legislatures.
causes: Garrison's rejection of gradual emancipation and colonization schemes
Second Great Awakening framing slavery as personal sin
Free black subscribers and financiers sustaining the paper
effects: Immediatism gained a durable national platform
Southern states banned the paper and offered rewards for Garrison's arrest
New England and American Anti-Slavery Societies founded in 1832 and 1833
significance: Shifted abolitionism from gradual reform to uncompromising moral demand
Published continuously for thirty-five years until slavery's legal end

title: Nat Turner's Rebellion
description: Enslaved preacher Nat Turner led a bloody organized slave uprising in Virginia, killing 60 white people.
cause: Turner's religious visions of divine retribution against the horrors of institutional chattel slavery.
effect: Mass executions of suspected rebels and passage of draconian black codes restricting education and assembly.
causes: Turner's religious visions of divine retribution against the horrors of institutional chattel slavery
effects: Mass executions of suspected rebels
Passage of draconian black codes restricting education and assembly
significance: Shattered the southern myth of the 'contented slave'
Intensified southern white defense of slavery

title: Nullification Crisis
description: South Carolina declared federal tariffs null, void, and non-binding within its state borders.
cause: The Tariff of Abominations hurt the Southern agrarian economy while fears grew of future federal interference with slavery.
effect: Jackson passed the Force Bill while Henry Clay negotiated a Compromise Tariff, and South Carolina backed down.
causes: High Tariff of Abominations hurting the Southern agrarian economy
Fear of future federal intervention against slavery
effects: Jackson passes Force Bill
Henry Clay negotiates a Compromise Tariff
South Carolina backs down
significance: Developed the radical states' rights constitutional arguments that would later justify Southern secession in 1860

title: Trail of Tears
description: Federal troops herded Cherokee families into stockades beginning in May 1838, then forced roughly 16,000 people west to Indian Territory over the following winter.
cause: The Treaty of New Echota, signed in 1835 by a small unauthorized faction, gave the government its legal pretext for removal.
effect: Around 4,000 Cherokee died of disease, exposure, and starvation in the camps and on the westward march.
causes: Treaty of New Echota signed by an unauthorized Cherokee minority
Georgia's seizure of Cherokee land after gold discoveries
Jackson and Van Buren refusing to enforce Worcester v. Georgia
effects: Roughly 4,000 Cherokee deaths from disease, exposure, and starvation
Cherokee Nation resettled in Indian Territory
Bitter internal rifts over the treaty, ending in the 1839 killings of its signers
significance: Completed the removal of the Southeast's major Native nations
Became the defining case of federal treaty violation and forced displacement

title: Annexation of Texas
description: The U.S. admitted the Lone Star Republic as a state via a joint resolution of Congress.
cause: The election of expansionist James K. Polk and Southern desire to add massive new territory for cotton cultivation.
effect: Caused a severe breakdown in diplomatic relations with Mexico and increased sectional tensions over slave state counts.
causes: Election of expansionist James K. Polk
Southern desire to add massive new territory for cotton cultivation
effects: Severe breakdown in diplomatic relations with Mexico
Increased sectional tensions over slave state counts
significance: Acted as the direct geopolitical trigger for the impending Mexican-American War

title: Mexican-American War
description: Armed conflict between the U.S. and Mexico fought across Texas, California, and Central Mexico.
cause: A boundary dispute at the Rio Grande, expansionist Manifest Destiny, and the desire for California ports.
effect: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo gave the U.S. the modern Southwest and reignited the debate over slavery's expansion.
causes: Boundary dispute at the Rio Grande
Expansionist zeal of Manifest Destiny
Desire for California ports
effects: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo
Mexican Cession gives U.S. the modern Southwest for $15 million
significance: Fulfilled the ocean-to-ocean territorial vision of Manifest Destiny
Reignited the toxic debate over slavery's expansion

title: Wilmot Proviso
description: A proposed legislative amendment sought to ban slavery in any territory acquired from Mexico.
cause: Northern Democratic resentment of Southern political dominance, aimed at territory the U.S. expected to win from the then-ongoing Mexican-American War.
effect: Passed the House repeatedly but failed in the Senate, with voting splitting strictly along sectional rather than party lines.
causes: Northern Democratic concerns over southern political dominance after the Mexican-American War
effects: Passes House repeatedly (northern majority) but fails in the Senate (sectional balance)
Voting splits strictly along sectional lines
significance: Signaled the collapse of traditional party loyalty
Replaced by toxic sectional polarization

title: California Gold Rush
description: Mass migration of 300,000 'Forty-Niners' rushed to California following gold discovery at Sutter's Mill.
cause: Accidental discovery of gold and economic desperation or desire for wealth among global migrants.
effect: Rapid population boom, devastation of indigenous populations, and California's application for statehood as a free state.
causes: Accidental discovery of gold
Economic desperation or desire for wealth among global migrants
effects: Rapid population boom
Devastation of indigenous populations
California applies for statehood as a free state
significance: Forced Congress to address the slavery expansion issue immediately
Led to the Compromise of 1850

title: Seneca Falls Convention
description: The first women's rights convention produced the Declaration of Sentiments demanding equality for women.
cause: Women reformers, many active in abolition, began applying democratic ideals to their own exclusion from public life.
effect: Launched the organized women's suffrage movement that culminated in the 19th Amendment in 1920.
causes: Women abolitionists were excluded from speaking at the 1840 World Anti-Slavery Convention
Reformers like Stanton applied the ideals of democracy to women's legal and political exclusion
effects: Adopted the Declaration of Sentiments, including the contested demand for the vote
Set off a wave of state and national women's rights conventions in the 1850s
Launched a 72-year campaign culminating in the 19th Amendment
significance: Marked the beginning of the organized women's rights movement in the United States
Applied the principles of the Declaration of Independence to argue for women's equality

title: Compromise of 1850
description: A series of acts admitted California as a free state and strengthened the Fugitive Slave Law.
cause: California's application for statehood after the Mexican-American War reignited the slavery extension debate.
effect: Temporarily delayed disunion but the Fugitive Slave Act intensified Northern opposition to slavery.
causes: California's gold rush population demanded statehood as a free state
Southern states demanded protections for slavery to balance the new free state
effects: The Fugitive Slave Act forced Northerners to participate in slavery enforcement
Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote Uncle Tom's Cabin in direct response
significance: Represented the last major sectional compromise before the Civil War
The Fugitive Slave Act converted many Northerners from indifference to active opposition to slavery

title: Publication of Uncle Tom's Cabin
description: Harriet Beecher Stowe's anti-slavery novel sold millions of copies and transformed northern public opinion on slavery.
cause: Stowe's moral outrage over the implementation of the new Fugitive Slave Act of 1850.
effect: Massive shift in northern public opinion toward abolition and intense anger and bans across the South.
causes: Stowe's moral outrage over the implementation of the new Fugitive Slave Act of 1850
effects: Massive shift in northern public opinion toward abolition
Intense anger and bans across the South
significance: Personalized the political abstractions of slavery
Turned it into an urgent moral issue for millions of ordinary citizens

title: Kansas-Nebraska Act
description: Congress repealed the Missouri Compromise and allowed popular sovereignty to determine slavery in new territories.
cause: Senator Stephen Douglas wanted to organize territories for a transcontinental railroad and proposed popular sovereignty.
effect: Led to 'Bleeding Kansas,' destroyed the Whig Party, and gave rise to the Republican Party.
causes: Douglas needed Southern support to organize the Nebraska territory for a northern railroad route
Popular sovereignty was his proposed compromise to avoid the Missouri Compromise line
effects: Bleeding Kansas turned the territory into a violent battleground between pro- and anti-slavery settlers
Destroyed the Whig Party and gave rise to the Republican Party
significance: Reopened the question of slavery's expansion that the Missouri Compromise had settled for 34 years
Directly led to the creation of the Republican Party and set the stage for Lincoln's rise

title: Dred Scott Decision
description: The Supreme Court ruled that African Americans were not citizens and Congress could not ban slavery in territories.
cause: Dred Scott sued for his freedom after living in free territories with his enslaved status intact.
effect: Outraged Northerners, emboldened Southerners, and pushed the nation closer to civil war.
causes: Scott argued that residing in free territories made him legally free
Scott's freedom suit, funded first by the Blow family and later taken up by antislavery attorneys
effects: Declared the Missouri Compromise unconstitutional, inflaming Northern opinion
Effectively declared that slavery could spread to all territories, making compromise impossible
significance: Widely considered one of the worst Supreme Court decisions in history
Pushed the nation irrevocably toward civil war by removing the possibility of legislative compromise on slavery

title: John Brown's Raid on Harpers Ferry
description: Radical abolitionist John Brown attempted to seize a federal arsenal to initiate an armed slave revolt.
cause: Brown's belief that slavery was a national sin that could only be purged through righteous bloodshed.
effect: Brown's capture and execution inspired northern mourning while triggering southern terror over northern complicity.
causes: Brown's belief that slavery was a national sin that could only be purged through righteous bloodshed
effects: Capture and execution of Brown
Northern mourning
Southern terror over northern complicity
significance: Convinced white southerners that northern republicans were actively plotting their physical destruction

title: Election of Abraham Lincoln
description: Republican candidate Lincoln won the presidency without winning a single southern state.
cause: A split within the Democratic Party and high Republican unity in the populous North.
effect: Secession of South Carolina rapidly followed by six other Deep South states forming the Confederacy.
causes: Split within the Democratic Party into Northern and Southern factions
High Republican unity in the populous North
effects: Secession of South Carolina
Rapidly followed by six other Deep South states to form the Confederacy
significance: The ultimate political tipping point that directly caused the outbreak of the American Civil War

title: Secession and the Firing on Fort Sumter
description: Six seceded states formed the Confederacy at Montgomery in February, joined by Texas in March, and in April Confederate batteries bombarded the federal garrison holding Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor.
cause: Lincoln's election in November 1860 convinced slaveholding states, starting with South Carolina that December, that they had permanently lost control of the federal government.
effect: The garrison surrendered after roughly 34 hours of shelling, and Lincoln's call for volunteers pushed four more states into the Confederacy.
causes: Lincoln's 1860 victory without a single Southern electoral vote
South Carolina's secession in December 1860, followed by six more states by February 1861
Lincoln's refusal to abandon federal forts and his decision to resupply Sumter
effects: Union garrison surrendered the fort on April 13, 1861
Lincoln called for 75,000 militia volunteers to suppress the rebellion
Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee, and North Carolina joined the Confederacy
significance: Opened the deadliest war in American history
Converted the constitutional argument over secession into a military contest

title: Homestead Act & Pacific Railway Act
description: Congress offered 160-acre plots to settlers who farmed them for five years and authorized the Union Pacific and Central Pacific to build a transcontinental railroad.
cause: Secession removed the Southern lawmakers who had long blocked free-soil homesteading and a northern railroad route, freeing Republicans to enact their development program.
effect: Federal land grants and bond subsidies triggered a surge of settlement and railroad construction across the trans-Mississippi West.
causes: Secession stripped Congress of Southern opposition to free-soil land policy
Republican free-labor vision of the West settled by small farmers
Wartime urgency to bind California and the Far West to the Union
effects: 160 acres offered for a filing fee and five years of residence
Union Pacific and Central Pacific received land grants and federal loans
Rapid acceleration of white settlement on the Great Plains
significance: Made the federal government the chief engine of western development
Set up decades of conflict with Plains Native nations over the same land

title: Battle of Gettysburg & the Gettysburg Address
description: Union forces repulsed Lee's invasion of Pennsylvania in a three-day July battle, and that November Lincoln spoke at the dedication of the soldiers' cemetery there.
cause: Lee gambled on a second invasion of the North, hoping a victory on Union soil would break Northern morale and win European recognition.
effect: Lee withdrew to Virginia with a crippled army while Lincoln's address recast the war as a test of government by the people.
causes: Lee's decision to carry the war onto Northern soil
Confederate hope that a defeat above the Potomac would force negotiations
Chance collision of the two armies at a Pennsylvania road junction
effects: Roughly 50,000 combined casualties over three days
Lee's army retreated and never again mounted a major invasion of the North
Lincoln's November 19 dedication speech redefined the war's purpose
significance: Paired with Vicksburg as the military turning point of the war
Bound Union victory to the Declaration's promise of equality

title: Emancipation Proclamation
description: President Lincoln declared enslaved people in Confederate states to be free as a war measure.
cause: Lincoln sought to weaken the Confederacy, energize Union troops, and deter European intervention on the South's behalf.
effect: Transformed the Civil War into a war for freedom and enabled African Americans to enlist in the Union Army.
causes: Military setbacks made Lincoln willing to use emancipation as a war strategy
Britain and France were considering recognizing the Confederacy; Lincoln wanted to make slavery the central issue
effects: Nearly 180,000 African Americans served in the Union Army
Prevented Britain and France from formally recognizing the Confederacy
significance: Transformed the Civil War's purpose from union to freedom
Paved the way for the 13th Amendment and the end of slavery

title: 13th Amendment Ratified
description: The amendment abolished slavery and involuntary servitude throughout the United States, except as punishment for a crime.
cause: Union victory and Republican determination to make emancipation permanent and constitutional rather than a wartime measure.
effect: Permanently ended legal slavery nationwide, freeing roughly four million people.
causes: Union victory in the Civil War
Emancipation Proclamation applied only to Confederate territory
Republican determination to make abolition permanent
effects: Slavery abolished nationwide
Roughly four million people freed
Southern states passed Black Codes to restrict the freed population
significance: Wrote abolition permanently into the Constitution
Set up the citizenship and voting fights of the 14th and 15th Amendments

title: Freedmen's Bureau Established
description: Congress created the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands inside the War Department to aid formerly enslaved people and destitute refugees across the ruined South.
cause: Emancipation and Union victory left millions of freedpeople without land, wages, schooling, or legal protection in a devastated region.
effect: Bureau agents distributed rations and medical care, supervised labor contracts, and helped establish thousands of schools for freedpeople.
causes: Roughly four million freedpeople emerged from slavery owning nothing
Wartime destruction and a vast refugee crisis across the South
Federal responsibility for abandoned and confiscated Confederate land
effects: Rations, medical care, and legal aid for freedpeople and refugees
Federal supervision of labor contracts between planters and freed workers
Thousands of schools founded, including colleges such as Howard University
significance: First large federal social welfare agency in American history
Laid the foundation of Black education in the South before Congress wound it down in 1872

title: Surrender at Appomattox Court House
description: General Robert E. Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia to General Ulysses S. Grant, effectively ending the Civil War.
cause: Total exhaustion of Confederate resources, Grant's relentless war of attrition, and the fall of Richmond.
effect: Collapse of the remaining Confederate armies and the end of armed Civil War military operations.
causes: Total exhaustion of Confederate resources
Grant's relentless war of attrition
Fall of Richmond
effects: Collapse of the remaining Confederate armies
End of armed Civil War military operations
significance: Preserved the constitutional union of states
Set the stage for the Reconstruction era

title: 14th Amendment Ratified
description: The amendment granted citizenship to formerly enslaved people and guaranteed equal protection under the law.
cause: Congress sought to enshrine the Civil Rights Act of 1866 in the Constitution to protect freedpeople's rights.
effect: Became the constitutional basis for civil rights decisions throughout the 20th century and beyond.
causes: Southern states passed Black Codes to effectively re-enslave freedpeople after the war
Congress needed constitutional protection for Black citizenship that could not be repealed by statute
effects: Overturned Dred Scott by granting citizenship to all born in the U.S.
Became the foundation for most 20th-century civil rights and civil liberties decisions
significance: Most important constitutional amendment since the Bill of Rights
The basis of nearly all modern civil rights law, from school desegregation to same-sex marriage

title: Transcontinental Railroad Completed
description: The Central Pacific and Union Pacific railroads met at Promontory Summit, Utah, connecting the continent by rail.
cause: The federal government funded construction to bind the nation together and facilitate western settlement.
effect: Accelerated industrialization, enabled mass western migration, and devastated Native American peoples and bison herds.
causes: Federal government issued land grants and loans to incentivize private railroad construction
Post-Civil War leaders saw a continental railroad as essential to national unity and economic growth
effects: Enabled mass settlement of the Great Plains, displacing Native American nations
Fueled industrial capitalism by integrating national markets
significance: Transformed the American economy by creating a truly national market
Accelerated the destruction of Native American cultures and bison herds of the Great Plains

title: 15th Amendment Ratified
description: Ratified on February 3, 1870, the amendment barred the federal government and the states from denying the vote based on race, color, or previous enslavement.
cause: Republicans wanted Black male suffrage secured in the Constitution rather than resting on statutes a future Congress could repeal.
effect: Constitutionalized the Black male franchise the Reconstruction Acts had already created in the South and extended it nationwide.
causes: Republican fear that Democratic victories would erase Black suffrage
Desire to extend Black voting beyond the occupied South to border and Northern states
Sustained pressure from Black activists and Radical Republicans
effects: Extended Black male suffrage to Northern and border states
Split the women's suffrage movement as it moved through Congress
Prompted Enforcement Acts aimed at Klan violence at the polls
significance: First constitutional guarantee of voting rights against racial discrimination
Left openings—poll taxes, literacy tests, violence—that disfranchised Black Southerners for generations

title: Battle of Little Bighorn
description: Lakota Sioux and Cheyenne warriors destroyed General Custer's 7th Cavalry in Montana.
cause: Encroachment of white gold miners into the sacred Black Hills in violation of the Treaty of Fort Laramie.
effect: A short-term native victory triggered the long-term retributive deployment of massive federal military force.
causes: Encroachment of white gold miners into the sacred Black Hills
Violation of the Treaty of Fort Laramie
effects: Short-term native victory
Long-term retributive deployment of massive federal military force
significance: Marked the high-water mark of native military resistance to the reservation system in the West

title: Compromise of 1877
description: An informal political deal awarded the contested 1876 presidency to Republican Rutherford B. Hayes in exchange for ending Reconstruction.
cause: Contested electoral votes in three Southern states and the threat of a renewed civil conflict over the election.
effect: Removal of all remaining federal troops from the South, returning unchecked white Democratic rule.
causes: Contested electoral votes in three Southern states
Threat of a renewed civil conflict over the election
effects: Removal of all remaining federal troops from the South
Return of unchecked white Democratic rule ('Redemption')
significance: Formally ended Reconstruction
Ushered in the era of Jim Crow segregation and Black disenfranchisement

title: Great Railroad Strike
description: A nationwide strike halted rail traffic and was crushed by federal troops sent by President Hayes.
cause: A third round of wage cuts in a year by major railroad companies during an economic depression.
effect: Over 100 deaths, destruction of rail property, and growth of organized union memberships.
causes: Third round of wage cuts in a year by major railroad companies during an economic depression
effects: Over 100 deaths
Destruction of rail property
Growth of organized union memberships
significance: The first major national labor strike in American history
Exposed the deep divide between industrial capital and labor

title: Chinese Exclusion Act
description: A federal law halted all immigration of Chinese laborers into the United States.
cause: White working-class resentment in California over wage competition and virulent nativism and racial scapegoating.
effect: Drastic decline in the Chinese-American population and establishment of a system of immigration tracking.
causes: White working-class resentment in California over wage competition
Virulent nativism and racial scapegoating
effects: Drastic decline in the Chinese-American population
Establishment of a system of immigration tracking
significance: The first federal immigration law to explicitly ban a specific ethnic group based entirely on race and nationality

title: Standard Oil Trust & the Rise of Big Business
description: John D. Rockefeller's lawyers placed dozens of allied oil companies under nine trustees, inventing a legal device that centralized control of an industry across state lines.
cause: State laws barred a corporation from holding stock in out-of-state firms, so Standard Oil needed a new structure to run its scattered holdings as one enterprise.
effect: The trust directed roughly nine-tenths of American oil refining and became the model that other industries quickly copied.
causes: Ruinous price competition among oil refiners
State laws blocking cross-state corporate ownership
Rockefeller's drive to absorb rivals through rebates and buyouts
effects: Nine trustees controlled about 90 percent of U.S. refining capacity
Sugar, whiskey, and tobacco producers adopted the same trust form
Public alarm over monopoly power intensified
significance: Defined the corporate consolidation that shaped the Gilded Age economy
Provoked the antitrust laws and business regulation of the Progressive Era

title: Haymarket Square Riot
description: A bomb was thrown at police during a labor rally in Chicago; police opened fire, killing workers.
cause: A strike at McCormick Reaper Works and labor mobilization demanding an 8-hour workday.
effect: Public associated unions with foreign anarchists, causing the rapid collapse of the Knights of Labor.
causes: Strike at McCormick Reaper Works
Labor mobilization demanding an 8-hour workday
effects: Public associates unions with foreign anarchists
Rapid collapse of the Knights of Labor union
significance: Dealt a near-fatal blow to the radical labor movement
Shifted dominance to the conservative American Federation of Labor (AFL)

title: Dawes Severalty Act
description: A law broke up communal tribal lands into individual private 160-acre farming plots to force assimilation.
cause: White reformist desires to forcibly assimilate Native Americans and corporate hunger for surplus reservation land.
effect: Loss of 90 million acres of tribal land and systemic destruction of native cultural structures.
causes: White reformist desires to forcibly assimilate Native Americans
Corporate hunger for surplus reservation land
effects: Loss of 90 million acres of tribal land
Systemic destruction of native cultural structures
significance: The centerpiece of federal assimilation policy
Designed to systematically dissolve native tribal identity

title: Sherman Antitrust Act
description: Congress passed the first federal law to limit monopolies and protect competitive markets.
cause: Public outrage over Standard Oil, railroads, and other trusts that fixed prices and crushed competition.
effect: Established the legal framework for antitrust enforcement, though weakly applied until the Progressive Era.
causes: The Gilded Age saw massive monopolistic trusts control oil, steel, and railroads
Farmers and small businesses demanded federal protection from price manipulation
effects: Created the legal basis for breaking up monopolies, though rarely enforced until TR
Gave future presidents a tool to challenge corporate power
significance: Extended federal regulation beyond railroads to the economy as a whole, asserting national authority over corporate consolidation
Laid the groundwork for the Progressive Era's trust-busting reforms

title: Wounded Knee Massacre
description: U.S. Army soldiers opened fire on a camp of Lakota Sioux, killing nearly 300 men, women, and children.
cause: White fear of the religious 'Ghost Dance' movement and tensions over the killing of Sitting Bull.
effect: Absolutely ended organized armed Native American resistance on the Great Plains.
causes: White fear of the religious 'Ghost Dance' movement
Tensions over the killing of Sitting Bull
effects: Absolute end of organized armed Native American resistance on the Great Plains
significance: Symbolized the tragic closing of the Indian Wars
Marked the final subjection of Native Americans

title: Ellis Island Opens & the "New Immigration"
description: The federal immigration station in New York Harbor opened on January 1, 1892, receiving arrivals who came increasingly from southern and eastern Europe.
cause: Congress had taken immigration control away from the states in 1891 and needed a federal depot to inspect the swelling volume of newcomers.
effect: Inspectors screened arrivals for disease and destitution, admitting the overwhelming majority and turning back a small fraction.
causes: Federal takeover of immigration inspection under the 1891 law
Closure of New York's state-run Castle Garden depot
Rising arrivals from Italy, Poland, Russia, and Austria-Hungary
effects: Medical and legal inspection of steerage passengers in New York Harbor
Growth of dense ethnic neighborhoods in Northeastern cities
Nativist demands for literacy tests and restriction grew louder
significance: Processed some twelve million immigrants before closing in 1954
Reshaped American ethnic and religious life, fueling the restriction laws of the 1920s

title: Homestead Strike
description: Steelworkers battled armed Pinkerton detectives at Andrew Carnegie's steel mill in Pennsylvania.
cause: Henry Clay Frick's 20% wage slash and his effort to smash the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers.
effect: State militia crushed the strike, leaders were blacklisted, and unionism was eliminated in steel for decades.
causes: Henry Clay Frick slashes wages by 20%
Effort to smash the powerful Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers
effects: State militia crushes the strike
Strike leaders blacklisted
Unionism eliminated in the steel industry for decades
significance: Demonstrated the absolute power of Gilded Age industrial corporations when backed by state authority

title: Populist Party Formed (Omaha Platform)
description: A third-party political convention demanded radical economic reforms for farmers and workers.
cause: High corporate railroad shipping rates, crushing debt caused by deflation, and lack of a responsive silver currency.
effect: Demanded free silver, a graduated income tax, government ownership of railroads, and direct election of senators.
causes: High corporate railroad shipping rates
Crushing debt caused by deflation
Lack of a responsive silver currency
effects: Demand for free silver, graduated income tax, government ownership of railroads, and direct election of senators
significance: The most successful agrarian third-party challenge in U.S. history
Its ideas were later adopted during the Progressive Era

title: Pullman Strike
description: Railroad workers boycotted Pullman luxury cars, halting western rail traffic before being ended by a federal court injunction.
cause: George Pullman cut wages during a depression while refusing to lower rents in his company town.
effect: Eugene V. Debs was jailed as President Cleveland deployed troops using mail delivery disruption as justification.
causes: George Pullman cuts wages during a depression
Refuses to lower rents in his company town
effects: Eugene V. Debs jailed
President Cleveland deploys troops using the excuse of mail delivery disruption
significance: Established the federal court injunction as a powerful legal weapon used by corporations to destroy strikes

title: Atlanta Compromise: Washington vs. Du Bois
description: Booker T. Washington told a mostly white Atlanta exposition audience that Black Southerners should build trades and property before pressing claims to social and political equality.
cause: Washington sought white support for Black economic advancement and for Tuskegee at a moment of spreading lynching, segregation, and disfranchisement.
effect: White politicians and Northern philanthropists embraced Washington as the recognized spokesman for Black America.
causes: Escalating lynching and legal segregation across the 1890s South
Southern states stripping Black men of the ballot
Washington's need for white funding to sustain Tuskegee Institute
effects: White press and donors hailed Washington as a national Black leader
Philanthropic money flowed toward industrial and vocational schooling
W. E. B. Du Bois attacked the bargain eight years later in The Souls of Black Folk (1903)
significance: Framed a decades-long debate over accommodation versus agitation
Du Bois's later opposition helped produce the Niagara Movement and the NAACP

title: Election of 1896 & the "Cross of Gold"
description: William Jennings Bryan's free-silver oratory captured the Democratic nomination, but Republican William McKinley's lavishly funded campaign carried the industrial North and the presidency.
cause: The depression that began in 1893 made the money supply the central political question, setting indebted farmers against creditors and industrialists.
effect: McKinley took 271 electoral votes to Bryan's 176, and the Populist Party collapsed after fusing behind the Democratic ticket.
causes: Depression of 1893 and collapsing crop prices
Farmer demands for inflation through free coinage of silver
Populist decision to fuse behind the Democratic nominee
effects: Bryan's Cross of Gold speech won him the nomination on the fifth ballot
Mark Hanna raised record corporate contributions for McKinley
Populism faded as an independent national movement
significance: Realigned national politics behind Republicans until the New Deal
Settled the currency fight in favor of the gold standard

title: Plessy v. Ferguson
description: The Supreme Court ruled that racially segregated public facilities did not violate the 14th Amendment.
cause: Homer Plessy deliberately challenged Louisiana's Separate Car Act via civil disobedience.
effect: The 'separate but equal' doctrine was established, enabling rapid expansion of Jim Crow laws.
causes: Homer Plessy deliberately challenges Louisiana's Separate Car Act via civil disobedience
effects: Establishment of the legal doctrine of 'separate but equal'
Rapid expansion of Jim Crow laws
significance: Provided federal constitutional protection for systemic, institutionalized racial segregation for over half a century

title: Spanish-American War
description: The U.S. defeated Spain in a brief war, gaining Guam, Puerto Rico, and the Philippines.
cause: Yellow journalism, the sinking of the USS Maine, and Cuban rebels' struggle for independence rallied U.S. public opinion.
effect: Launched the United States as an imperial power with overseas territories and global military commitments.
causes: Yellow journalism by Hearst and Pulitzer inflamed public opinion against Spain
American business interests in Cuba and strategic interest in Pacific trade routes
effects: U.S. acquired its first overseas empire: Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines
Teller Amendment kept Cuba out of U.S. hands, leaving it a protectorate under the Platt Amendment
Sparked the Philippine-American War as Filipinos resisted American colonialism
significance: Marked the United States' emergence as a global imperial power
Created ongoing moral debates about American colonialism that echo today

title: Open Door Policy
description: The U.S. issued diplomatic notes demanding equal trading access to China for all the major powers, including Japan alongside Britain, Germany, Russia, France, and Italy.
cause: American fear of being locked out of Chinese markets by European spheres of influence.
